lesson.title: Acquisition: How a New Response Gets Built
lesson.summary: Acquisition is the learning phase of classical conditioning, the period during which a neutral stimulus is paired repeatedly with an unconditioned stimulus until it starts triggering the response on its own.
lesson.body:
Before any conditioning has happened, an organism already reacts automatically to certain stimuli. Pavlov called that automatic reaction an unconditioned response, and the stimulus that reliably triggers it an unconditioned stimulus. Food in a dog's mouth automatically causes salivation, no learning required. Acquisition is the name for what happens when a stimulus that used to mean nothing, a neutral stimulus, gets paired with that unconditioned stimulus often enough that it starts to trigger a similar response all by itself. Once that transfer has happened, the once neutral stimulus is called the conditioned stimulus, and the response it now produces is the conditioned response.

Pavlov's dogs are the classic case. In his lab, a sound, commonly described in textbooks as a bell, though Pavlov actually used a range of auditory cues in his experiments, including a metronome, was played just before food was delivered to the dogs. Early on, the sound alone did nothing. But after enough pairings, the sound started to make the dogs salivate even when no food appeared. That is acquisition in action: the sound has gone from neutral stimulus to conditioned stimulus, and the salivation it now produces on its own is the conditioned response.

Timing matters more than most people expect. Conditioning is strongest when the neutral stimulus appears shortly before the unconditioned stimulus, so the organism can use it as a signal that something important is about to happen. If the two are presented far apart in time, or if the neutral stimulus comes after the unconditioned stimulus rather than before it, learning is much weaker or may not happen at all. Acquisition also is not usually instant. The conditioned response typically grows stronger over repeated pairings until it levels off, at which point the association is considered learned. That learned association is the foundation for everything else in classical conditioning, including what happens when the pairings stop, which is where extinction comes in.
